section.title: Knowing God by Obedience
section.sectionRationale: John gives the first great test of true faith: we can be sure we know God if we keep His commandments and walk as Jesus walked. He shows that the old command to love is also new in Christ, that hating a brother is to remain in darkness, and he reassures his readers by their standing in Christ.
section.thesis: Assurance that we truly know God is confirmed by keeping His commandments and walking as Jesus walked, and above all by loving our brothers, for the one who hates walks in darkness while the one who loves remains in the light in which Christ has already secured them.
section.frameNote: Three beats: knowing God confirmed by obedience; the old yet new command to love, with light against the darkness of hatred; and words of assurance to children, fathers, and young men.

units.label: Knowing Him by keeping His commandments

verses.text: By this we can be sure that we have come to {{ginosko|know}} Him: if we {{tereo|keep}} His {{entole|commandments}}.
If anyone says, “I know Him,” but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
But if anyone keeps His word, the {{agape|love}} of God has been truly {{teleioo|perfected}} in him. By this we know that we are in Him:
Whoever claims to {{meno|abide}} in Him must walk as Jesus walked.
Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning. This commandment is the message you have heard.
Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining.
If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness.
Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him.
But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

units.label: Words of assurance
units.note: to children, fathers, and young men

verses.text: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name.

I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have {{nikao|overcome}} the evil one. I have written to you, children, because you know the Father.

I have written to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

ginosko.gloss: To know, often by experience and relationship, not merely by information. To know God in this sense is to be in living fellowship with Him. John says this real knowing shows itself in a life of obedience; a claim to know God without obedience is empty.

tereo.gloss: To keep, guard, observe, hold fast. To keep His commandments is not cold rule-keeping but treasuring and obeying what God has said out of love. It is the fruit and evidence of truly knowing Him, not the means of earning His favour.

entole.gloss: Commandment, instruction, charge. In this letter the commandments centre on believing in Christ and loving one another. Keeping them is the mark of those who know God, and John will show that love is the heart of what God commands.

agape.gloss: Love, especially self-giving love that seeks the good of another. The love of God can mean His love for us, our love for Him, or both together; it is brought to its goal, perfected, in the one who keeps His word. This love is the pulse of the whole letter.

teleioo.gloss: To complete, bring to its goal, make perfect in the sense of mature and fully realised. When we keep God's word, His love reaches its intended end in us. It speaks of love coming to full expression, not of sinless flawlessness.

meno.gloss: To remain, abide, dwell, continue. A key word in John for the settled, ongoing union between the believer and Christ. To abide in Him is to stay in living fellowship with Him, and the proof of that claim is walking as Jesus walked.

nikao.gloss: To conquer, overcome, be victorious. John tells the young men they have overcome the evil one because the word of God abides in them. The victory is real and already won in Christ, giving grounds for assurance in the fight against sin and error.

basic.context: How can you know you really know God? John gives a plain test: those who truly know Him keep His commandments and live the way Jesus lived. He is not talking about earning God's love but about the fruit that proves it is real. The command he keeps returning to is love. To claim to be in the light while hating a fellow believer is to be in the dark. Then he reassures his readers with what is already true of them in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a test of assurance, not a ladder to salvation. Obedience and love are the evidence that we have come to know God, not the price of knowing Him. John writes tenderly, calling his readers little children, fathers, and young men, and reminding them their sins are forgiven and the evil one is overcome, so the test builds confidence rather than crushing it.
basic.originalLanguages: To know, ginosko, God is to be in living fellowship with Him, shown by keeping, tereo, His commandments, entole. When we keep His word the love, agape, of God is perfected, teleioo, brought to its goal, in us. To abide, meno, in Him is to walk as Jesus walked, and John assures the young men they have overcome, nikao, the evil one.
basic.typology: The old commandment given at the beginning and made new in Christ echoes the law given to Israel, now fulfilled and deepened in Jesus, who loved to the end. The true light already shining is the dawn of the promised new age in Christ, breaking on the fading darkness.
basic.christ: Jesus is the pattern, whoever abides in Him must walk as He walked, and He is the substance of the command, the love that fulfils the law. He is the true light already shining, and it is through His name that sins are forgiven, the ground of all the assurance John gives.
basic.god: God is knowable, and He is known truly in a life of obedient love. He is the God whose love comes to its goal in His people, who forgives sins through His Son's name, and who is called both the One from the beginning and the Father, drawing His children into secure fellowship.
basic.crossReferences: John 13:34 gives the new commandment to love as Jesus loved. John 14:15 says if you love Me you will keep My commandments. John 15 speaks of abiding in Christ, and Leviticus 19:18 is the old command to love your neighbour.
basic.oneStory: The old command to love, first given long ago, becomes new in Jesus, who kept it perfectly and pours His love into His people. As the true light dawns, God's children walk as Jesus walked and love one another, living proof that they have come to know the God the whole story reveals.

context.literary:
This section of the letter is built on a pattern of three claims. Three times John introduces a person by the same words, "the one who says." "If anyone says, 'I know Him,'" verse 4; "Whoever claims to abide in Him," verse 6; "If anyone claims to be in the light," verse 9. Each claim is a boast about a relationship with God, and each is tested by conduct: keeping His commandments, walking as Jesus walked, loving a brother. The three tests are really one, since obedience, imitation of Christ and love are three views of the same life. The first two tests are stated in positive and negative form, and the third has its own positive and negative: whoever loves remains in the light, whoever hates is in darkness, verses 10 and 11.

The verses on the old and new commandment, 7 to 8, stand like a hinge in the middle. John says he is not writing a new commandment, then says that he is. The paradox is deliberate. The commandment is old because it has been the message since the beginning, and new because its truth has now been displayed in Christ and in the lives of believers, and because the darkness is already giving way. The light imagery of 1:5 returns here and now includes movement: the darkness is passing, the true light is already shining.

Verses 12 to 14 change the key. After the sharp tests, John stops to address his readers with six short statements arranged as two sets of three, one group in the present tense "I am writing," and one in the past, "I have written." Each set speaks to children, fathers and young men. The poetry is not an afterthought: it is a pastoral reassurance that the tests of verses 3 to 11 are not meant to unsettle the believers. The section moves from examination to affirmation, and it does so on purpose.
context.historical:
The language of knowing God was in the air of the first century. Greek religion and philosophy prized knowledge, and the movements that later grew into Gnosticism taught that salvation came through special insight. We should not read the full second-century systems back into this letter, but the description in 1 John fits a community in which some claimed a superior knowledge of God while setting aside ordinary obedience and love. The letter says plainly that those who left did not belong, 1 John 2:19, and that they denied the Son, 1 John 2:22.

John's answer is rooted in the Old Testament's understanding of knowledge. In Hebrew thought, to know God is not only to have information but to be in a relationship that shapes a life. Jeremiah says that the king Josiah judged the cause of the poor and needy, and asks, "Is that not what it means to know Me?" Jeremiah 22:16. The New Covenant promise is that God will put His law in their minds and write it on their hearts, and that all will know Him, Jeremiah 31:33 to 34. Ezekiel adds that God will put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His statutes, Ezekiel 36:27. John reads his own community as the place where these promises are being fulfilled, and he treats obedience as the sign.

The three groups in verses 12 to 14 are probably not strict age brackets but ways of speaking to the whole church. "Little children" is John's usual affectionate term for all his readers, 1 John 2:1 and 2:28. "Fathers" and "young men" are likely pictures of maturity and strength. Whether he addresses literal ages or the whole community in different aspects, the effect is the same: every kind of believer has something true to hold.
context.canonical:
The central commandment of the passage is love, and its roots go deep. Moses told Israel, "Love your neighbor as yourself," Leviticus 19:18, and Jesus said that the whole law and the prophets hang on loving God and loving one's neighbor, Matthew 22:37 to 40. At the Last Supper He called love a "new commandment," "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another," John 13:34, and John's puzzle of an old and new commandment follows from that. The command is old because it is as old as the law, and new because it now carries the measure of Christ's own love. Paul takes the same step: love is the fulfillment of the law, Romans 13:8 to 10 and Galatians 5:14.

The link between loving God and keeping His commands is stated in the Gospel too. "If you love Me, you will keep My commandments," John 14:15; "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love," John 15:10, and the one who keeps them is the one who loves Him, John 14:21. John returns to the point in 1 John 5:3 and in 2 John 5 and 6, where love and walking according to the commandments are one and the same.

The light and darkness language continues from John 1:5 and 8:12, and the blinding of verse 11 recalls the language of John 12:40, which quotes Isaiah 6. The message of the passage about the one who hates his brother also looks ahead to 1 John 3:14 and 4:20, where the logic is stated plainly: one who does not love the brother he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. The tests of this section are taken up and developed through the rest of the letter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted his readers to be able to tell the difference between real and counterfeit Christianity without being thrown into anxiety. The letter's opponents offered a confident claim to know God, and the believers who stayed behind might have felt that their own faith looked plain beside it. John answers by giving them marks that cannot be faked for long: obedience, imitation of Christ, and love for fellow believers. These are the ordinary fruit of a life that has been joined to God, and any believer who finds them growing in himself has reason for confidence.

He also meant to claim the word "know" for ordinary believers. The false teachers treated knowledge as an elite possession; John says that every child in the family knows the Father, 2:13, and that the word of God abides in the young men, 2:14. Knowing God is the common inheritance of all who have been forgiven, and its proof is a changed life, not a higher level of secret insight.

Finally, John wanted to make love the visible center. When he says the commandment is old and new at once, he is telling his readers that nothing they have not already been taught is required of them, and that nothing they have already been taught is outdated. The test of whether they stand in the light is the same as it has always been, and they are meant to take it as a gift that lets them recognize themselves as people the darkness has begun to lose.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The section is written as a series of tests, and tests can be misused in two ways. One is to use them on others, as a checklist for judging whether a neighbor is truly saved. John writes them for his own readers to use on themselves in light of a specific crisis, and he is careful to say, immediately after, that his readers have been forgiven and have overcome. The other misuse is to treat obedience as a condition we meet in order to earn God's love. The text says the opposite: the love of God is perfected in the one who keeps His word, which means that obedience is where love comes to its full growth, not where it begins. The reason we love is that God first loved us, 1 John 4:19.

The commands in the passage are plain. Keep His commandments, walk as Jesus walked, love your brother. These are instructions for believers now. The conditions in verses 9 to 11 are descriptive: they say what hatred and love reveal about a person's state. They are not a mandate to pronounce on anyone's final condition. A believer who finds hatred in his heart should hear a call to repent and return to the light, not a verdict that he was never in it.

It is also worth noting that "keep His commandments" does not mean sinless perfection, since the letter has just said that if anyone sins we have an advocate. The commitment is to a direction of life, with forgiveness for the stumbles.

debates.question: Is the assurance John offers based on works?

views.label: Assurance comes from the evidence of a changed life
views.case: John says 'by this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments,' verse 3, and 'by this we know that we are in Him,' verse 5. Many Reformed and evangelical readers take these as the 'fruits' that confirm a faith already given, in line with James 2:17 and the Reformers' teaching that justification is by faith alone but never by a faith that is alone.

views.label: Assurance rests on Christ and the Spirit, with works as a secondary sign
views.case: Others stress that the letter gives several grounds of assurance, including the confession that Jesus is the Christ and the testimony of the Spirit, 1 John 4:2 and 5:13, and that forgiveness is 'through His name,' 2:12. Obedience confirms but does not create the ground.

views.label: The test is aimed at the false teachers, not at doubting believers
views.case: Some stress that the tests were first written to expose the opponents and are not meant to be used by sensitive consciences to torment themselves. The following verses of comfort, 12 to 14, show the pastoral aim.

debates.bearing: The letter as a whole sets the tests inside the gospel of forgiveness: the first thing John says to his readers in this section is that their sins are forgiven through His name. Whichever emphasis one takes, the tests are meant to give confidence, not to take it away.

debates.question: Is the old and new commandment the same commandment, and why 'new'?

views.label: It is new because of Christ's example
views.case: The commandment to love is old, found in Leviticus 19:18, but Jesus gave it a new standard in His own love, John 13:34, and so it is new in Him. John adds that it is 'true in Him and also in you.'

views.label: It is new because of the new age
views.case: The reason John gives is that the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining. The new age has dawned, and what was a commandment under the old order is now lived in the power of the Spirit and the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33.

views.label: It is new in freshness, not in content
views.case: Some think the Greek word for 'new' here points to quality rather than time: it is renewed rather than recent. The commandment is the same one given from the beginning, now seen fresh in Christ.

debates.bearing: All three views see the command as the same love, deepened by Christ. The disagreement concerns where to place the newness, and the passage itself holds both: it is old because it has been the message, and new because the light has now come.

debates.question: What do 'children, fathers, young men' mean, and why do the statements repeat?

views.label: Three stages of spiritual maturity
views.case: Many take the groups as describing the newly converted, the mature, and the strong in battle. 'Fathers' know Him who is from the beginning, 'young men' have overcome the evil one, and 'children' know the Father and have been forgiven.

views.label: Different names for the whole church
views.case: Others hold that John is not distinguishing groups but using vivid titles for every believer, as he does elsewhere when he addresses all as 'little children,' 2:1 and 2:28. The repetition is rhetorical.

views.label: The repetition refers to the letter itself
views.case: The change from 'I am writing' to 'I have written' puzzles readers. Some think it refers to what John has already written in this letter, and others to a former letter or to the same letter from the perspective of the reader. The BSB leaves both forms in place.

debates.bearing: The meaning is the same under all three views: each kind of believer has something certain, and John writes to affirm it before he goes on to warn again in the verses that follow.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 uses the perfect tense for "know," egnokamen, so the sense is "we have come to know and so we know," a relationship begun and continuing. The verb ginosko in John's writings means more than information; it is the knowing of experience, as in John 17:3, "that they may know You, the only true God." The test of that knowing is the keeping of His commandments, and the verb for "keep," tereo, is in the present tense, "keep on keeping." Tereo means to guard or watch over, and in John's Gospel it is used of keeping Jesus' word, John 8:51 and 14:23, so that the picture is of treasuring as well as obeying. The word for commandment, entole, is used in the singular and plural in this letter and is the word Jesus used of His own instructions to the disciples, John 14:15.

Verse 5 says that in the one who keeps His word "the love of God has been truly perfected." The verb teteleiotai, from teleioo, is the perfect passive of a word that means to bring to completion, to reach the goal, telos. It does not mean flawless; it means brought to maturity. The phrase "love of God" is a genitive that the grammar leaves open: it could be God's love for us, our love for God, or love of the kind that belongs to God. Most readers see all three, since the same word is used in 4:12 and 4:17 of love "perfected in us."

Verse 6 says "whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked." The verb meno, "abide" or "remain," is one of John's favorite words for the settled relationship with Christ, as in John 15:4 to 10. The word "must" translates opheilei, "owes" or "is obligated," a word from the vocabulary of debt, so abiding creates an obligation of likeness. "As Jesus walked" uses ekeinos, "that One," which John uses elsewhere to point to Christ as the standard, as in 1 John 3:3, 3:5 and 3:7. The verb "walked" is in the aorist, a summary look at the whole of Jesus' life.

In verse 8 the commandment is new, kaine, and the darkness "is passing away," paragetai, in the present tense. The same verb appears in 2:17, where the world is "passing away." Two things are on the move: the darkness and the world, while the one who does the will of God remains. The Greek words for new, kainos and neos, differ: kainos tends to carry the sense of new in kind or freshness, while neos tends to carry the sense of recent in time, though the distinction should not be pressed in every case.

"Hates," misōn, in verses 9 and 11 is a present participle, a settled attitude. Verse 11 says darkness "has blinded" his eyes, etuphlosen, an aorist, and John 12:40 uses the same verb for the blinding of those who would not believe. The result is that the one who hates "does not know where he is going." In the next section "overcome," nenikekate, is perfect: "you have overcome and the victory stands." The same word returns in 4:4 and 5:4 and 5:5.

typology.type: The law written on stone and the law written on the heart
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai God gave commandments on tablets of stone, and Israel promised to obey, Exodus 24:3. The prophets saw that the heart was the problem, and Jeremiah promised a covenant in which God's law would be put in their minds and inscribed on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel promised a new heart and God's Spirit causing His people to walk in His statutes, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. John treats the keeping of the commandments as the result of that promise. The escalation is that what the law demanded from outside the Spirit now produces from inside. The limit of the type is that the old covenant could command but could not give the power to keep what it commanded.

typology.type: The pillar of light on the wilderness road
typology.fulfillment: Israel traveled by a pillar of fire that gave light by night, Exodus 13:21, and was kept from stumbling in the dark. John's 'the true light is already shining' and the one who loves 'remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him' take up the same picture of a people led by light so that they know where they are going. The fulfillment is that the light is Christ Himself, John 8:12, who said that whoever follows Him will not walk in darkness. The type's limit is that the pillar guided one nation across a desert, while the true Light shines for people everywhere.

typology.type: The exodus passover and the forgiveness of children
typology.fulfillment: On the night of the Passover the blood of the lamb covered each household, and the firstborn were spared, Exodus 12:13. John tells his readers that their sins 'have been forgiven through His name.' The pattern is that a household was safe because of what had been done, not because of its own merit, and the deliverance was followed by a life of obedience to the God who rescued them, Exodus 20:2. The escalation is that Christ is the Lamb, 1 Peter 1:19, and the forgiveness is for sin, not only for death. The picture is limited in that Passover protected one people for a night, while Christ's blood forgives sin for all time, Hebrews 10:14.

study.christ:
Christ appears in this section as the pattern, the substance, the light and the ground. He is the pattern: whoever claims to abide in Him "must walk as Jesus walked." The Gospels show what that walking looked like, from the Father's will as His food, John 4:34, to the washing of the disciples' feet, John 13:14 to 15, to laying down His life, 1 John 3:16. John does not say "be like Jesus" in a general sense. He says that the shape of the believer's life is to match the shape of Jesus' own, which is a life of obedience to the Father and love for others.

He is the substance of the commandment. The old command to love is new "in Him." John's Gospel gives the account: "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another," John 13:34. The measure of love is no longer the self, as in Leviticus 19:18, but Christ's own giving. The law's demands are not abandoned but filled out in a person, and Paul can say that love is the fulfillment of the law, Romans 13:10.

He is the light. When John says the true light is already shining, the phrase echoes the Gospel's "The true Light who gives light to every man was coming into the world," John 1:9, and Jesus' word "I am the light of the world," John 8:12. The dawning of the new age is not an abstract change in the times but the coming of a person. The darkness is fading because He has come and is coming.

He is the ground of forgiveness. The first statement of reassurance is that sins "have been forgiven through His name." In Scripture a name stands for the person and what He has done. Peter says that there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12, and John's own Gospel was written that people may have life in His name, John 20:31. The confidence of the believer rests here, before any mention of obedience.

Last, He is the victor. The young men have overcome the evil one, and elsewhere John tells us that the Son of God was revealed to destroy the works of the devil, 1 John 3:8, and that the one who is in believers is greater than the one in the world, 1 John 4:4. The overcoming is theirs only because it is His.

It would be a mistake to treat the old and new commandment as a riddle with a hidden Christ solution. Christ is not hidden here; John names Him in the verses that precede and follow, and the passage is about the life that comes from knowing Him.
study.god:
The God of this passage is a God who can be known. John does not hedge. He says "we know Him" and "you know the Father," and he uses the language of a relationship that has been established. This stands against every idea that God is a remote principle, and also against the idea that knowledge of Him is reserved for the few. The Father is known by children, which is to say by the youngest and simplest of believers, and He is known by fathers in their long experience. Knowing God is the ordinary condition of the forgiven.

He is also a God who gives commandments and means them. The passage says that keeping His word is the evidence of knowing Him. This is not because God is a demanding master but because He is a Father whose will is good. John says elsewhere that His commandments are not burdensome, 1 John 5:3. The commandments reveal His character, and obedience is a way of agreeing with who He is. The love of God is perfected in the person who keeps His word because the love and the word are the same thing seen from two sides.

The passage reveals God as the one who is making the darkness pass. The old order of sin and blindness is not permanent. John's verb is in the present tense: the darkness is passing away, and the true light is already shining. This tells us something about God's rule. He is not waiting passively for the end; He is at work now, and the signs of that work are visible in the lives of those who love. The same God who will bring a new heaven and a new earth is already creating a people who walk in the light.

He is a God who forgives before He demands. The first reassurance comes before the final test: sins are forgiven. His grace precedes and underlies His commands, in the same order as the Ten Commandments, which begin with "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt," Exodus 20:2, and then give the commands. The order shows how God relates to His people: He rescues first, and then He calls them to live as the rescued.

Finally, He is a God who defends His people against the evil one. The young men have overcome, and they are strong because the word of God abides in them. God's word is not only a command but a power at work. For worship, this teaches thankfulness for a knowledge of God that is not earned and gratitude for a word that does what it says.

crossReferences.note: In the upper room Jesus ties affection to action with an if and a then. The saying is the root of John's test: obedience is how devotion to Christ shows itself, and the letter simply restates the Master's own order of things.

Keeping Jesus' commandments is how believers remain in His love, just as He kept the Father's commandments and remains in His love. The verse shows the pattern behind the call to walk as Jesus walked: His own life of obedience is the model.

A new commandment, to love one another as Jesus has loved us, by which everyone will know we are His disciples. This is the source of the old and new commandment in 1 John 2:7 and 8, and it names the measure of the love John has in mind.

Love your neighbor as yourself. The command is the old commandment in its Old Testament form. John's claim that the commandment has been there from the beginning rests on laws like this one, which are older than any controversy in the church.

God promises to put His law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. The verse is the prophetic background to obedience as the mark of knowing God: in the new covenant the commandments are written within, and keeping them is the fruit.
Love fulfills the law, since love does no wrong to a neighbor. Paul reaches the same conclusion as John by another route, so that the apostles agree about what the commandment is.

Whoever says he loves God but hates his brother is a liar, because he cannot love the unseen God if he does not love the brother he has seen. The verse is the sharpest statement of the test of 2:9 to 11 and shows where John takes it later in the letter.

We know we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers. John restates the connection between light, life and love, and adds that the one who does not love remains in death. It makes the stakes of 2:9 to 11 explicit.

Later in the letter John defines love for God by obedience and adds that the orders carry no crushing weight. This answers any worry that the tests of chapter 2 impose a burden, and shows that the commandments are the shape of love, given by a Father who wants His children to flourish.

The commandment is not new but one from the beginning: that we love one another, and love is walking according to His commandments. The short letter repeats the old and new commandment and ties love and obedience into one, in nearly the same language as 1 John 2:7.

The Son of God was revealed to destroy the works of the devil. The verse stands behind the confidence that the young men have overcome the evil one, and shows that their victory rests on what Christ has done.

Believers were once darkness but are now light in the Lord, and are to walk as children of light. Paul describes the same transition from darkness to light that John says is under way, and uses the same word for walking.

study.oneStory:
The question "how do we know that we know God?" has been asked in every age of the story. In the garden the man and woman knew God and then hid from Him, and from that point knowing Him was something people had to be brought back to. At Sinai God said who He was and how His people should live, and Israel's life was meant to display the character of the God who had rescued them. Again and again the prophets said that Israel claimed to know Him while living in injustice and cruelty, and that real knowledge of God showed itself in care for the poor, as in Jeremiah 22:16.

The gap between the claim and the life is the problem of the whole Old Testament, and the promise of a new covenant is God's answer to it. He would write His law on their hearts, put His Spirit within them, forgive their sins, and make all of them know Him, Jeremiah 31:33 to 34 and Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. The passage in 1 John is a description of that promise coming true. Those who have been forgiven through His name know the Father; those in whom the word abides have overcome the evil one; and the sign of it all is that they keep His commandments and love one another.

The old and new commandment ties the whole story together. Love is at the root of the law, Leviticus 19:18, it is brought to its full measure in Christ, John 13:34, and it is lived by the Spirit's power in the church, so that the world can see who belongs to Jesus. The one who loves his brother "remains in the light." In the context of the larger story, this is what the people of God have been called to be from the beginning: a community in which the character of God is visible.

The passage also looks ahead. The darkness is "passing away," and the world is "passing away" with its desires, but the one who does the will of God remains forever, 1 John 2:17. That is the direction of the whole Bible: the darkness that came in at the fall is being undone, and the new creation will be a world in which there is no night and no hatred. Those who walk in the light now are already living the life of that world, and the love that marks them is the one thing that will never pass away. Paul says it plainly: "love never fails," 1 Corinthians 13:8. The story that began with a broken relationship ends with people who know God fully, as they are fully known, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

sermon.title: Keeping His Commands
sermon.why: Begg preaches this passage, 1 John 2:3-11, on the test of truly knowing God by keeping His commandments and loving the brothers, walking as Jesus walked. A clear, orthodox handling of assurance and obedience.

quiz.q: How can we be sure we have come to know God, according to verse 3?

options.text: By keeping His commandments as the evidence of a real relationship.
options.note: Obedience is the fruit that confirms true knowledge of God, not the price of it.

options.text: By feeling deeply religious most of the time.
options.note: Feelings can accompany faith, but the test John gives is obedience.

options.text: By earning God's acceptance through flawless performance.
options.note: Obedience is evidence, not the basis; forgiveness rests on Christ's name and work.

options.text: By gaining a superior, hidden knowledge of spiritual things.
options.note: John opposes claims to secret knowledge; the mark is obedient love, not esoteric insight.

quiz.q: What does John say about anyone who claims to know God but does not keep His commandments?

options.text: He is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
options.note: Verse 4 flatly exposes a claim to know God that is contradicted by disobedience.

options.text: He is simply a weaker but genuine believer.
options.note: John's language is stronger; the settled claim without obedience is false.

options.text: He knows God in a different but equally valid way.
options.note: John allows no valid knowledge of God divorced from obedience.

options.text: He needs only more information to believe rightly.
options.note: The problem is not lack of information but a claim contradicted by life.

quiz.q: Why does John call the command both old and new?

options.text: It is old, given from the beginning, yet made new and fulfilled in Christ as the light dawns.
options.note: Verses 7 and 8: the ancient command to love is renewed in Jesus who loved to the end.

options.text: It is old and therefore no longer binding on believers.
options.note: John does not set it aside; he presses it as the living command to love.

options.text: It is entirely new, with no roots in earlier revelation.
options.note: He calls it old too, rooted from the beginning; both are true, but this half misses the old.

options.text: It is a rule that has nothing to do with Jesus.
options.note: It is true in Him and shaped by His love; it is deeply tied to Jesus.

quiz.q: What does hating a fellow believer reveal, according to verses 9 to 11?

options.text: That the person is still in the darkness, however much they claim the light.
options.note: Hatred exposes a claim to be in the light as false; the hater walks blind in darkness.

options.text: That the person is in the light but struggling.
options.note: John says such a person is still in darkness, not merely struggling in the light.

options.text: That love and hatred make no real difference.
options.note: The whole passage makes love the decisive mark of walking in the light.

options.text: That the person simply needs to try to be nicer.
options.note: The issue is deeper than niceness; hatred reveals a heart still in darkness.

quiz.q: Why does John remind his readers of what is already true of them in verses 12 to 14?

options.text: To reassure them: their sins are forgiven and they have overcome the evil one in Christ.
options.note: The tests are set within strong assurance grounded in Christ's finished work.

options.text: To make them anxious about whether they measure up.
options.note: The tone is assurance, not anxiety; he reminds them of grace already given.

options.text: To flatter them into ignoring their sin.
options.note: John never excuses sin; he grounds real assurance in Christ, not flattery.

options.text: To single out only the mature as true believers.
options.note: He addresses children, fathers, and young men alike; assurance is for all, not only the mature.

questions: John says we can be sure we know God if we keep His commandments. How do you tell the difference between obedience as evidence of grace and obedience as an attempt to earn it?
To abide in Christ is to walk as Jesus walked. In what part of your life this week would walking as Jesus walked look most different from how you are living now?
The command John keeps returning to is love. Is there a fellow believer you find hard to love, and what would it mean to step out of that darkness into the light?
John reassures his readers that their sins are forgiven and the evil one is overcome. How does resting in what is already true of you in Christ fuel obedience rather than replace it?
The true light is already shining and the darkness is fading. Where do you see that light breaking into your own habits, relationships, and desires?

translationNotes.note: 'The love of God' is a genitive that can mean God's love for us, our love for God, or both; John's usage across the letter suggests God's love coming to its goal in the obedient believer.
'The darkness is fading and the true light is already shining' uses present tenses to picture the overlap of the ages, the new age dawning in Christ while the old darkness passes.

The shift from 'I am writing' to 'I have written' in verses 13 and 14 is likely stylistic emphasis rather than a change of meaning; the BSB footnote notes 'overcome the evil one' can read 'overcome evil'.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 John 2:3-14. Verse 13 line breaks joined with spaces; Footnote on 2:13 ('overcome evil') noted.
